newsitem.title: USA: Indiana tax assessment case sent back to tax court.
newsitem.headline: Indiana tax assessment case sent back to tax court.

text.p: The Indiana Supreme Court this week tossed the state's method of assessing property taxes back to the state tax court to determine whether the system results in "unjust and discriminatory valuation and assessment of real property."
In a ruling Monday, the high court reversed a May 31 decision by the Indiana Tax Court that found the system to be unconstitutional because it was not based solely on fair market valuation.
However, the Supreme Court affirmed the tax court's contention that the state legislature must provide "for a uniform and equal rate of property assessment and taxation based on property wealth."
The state's high court returned the case to the tax court to determine whether the current system results in non-uniform and unequal property valuations.
The Supreme Court also vacated a tax court order giving the state until March 1, 1998 to fix the current assessment system, which relies largely on calculating the replacement value of property.

Lawyers from the Indiana Civil Liberties Union, which is representing taxpayers and a town in northwest Indiana that filed the lawsuit, were not available to comment on the high court's ruling. A deputy Indiana attorney general, who was defending the Indiana Board of Tax Commissioners in the case, was also not available.
In the wake of the tax court ruling, Indiana lawmakers had been gearing up to tackle the state's property assessment system during their upcoming legislative session.

In June, Moody's Investors Service said a ruling finding Indiana's property assessment system to be unconstitutional could have longer-term credit implications for debt given changes the state would have to undertake to fix the system.
